title: Reversible metabolic arrest after traumatic exsanguination cardiac arrest

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an emergency preservation procedure for a patient whose heart has stopped because of catastrophic blood loss. It would rapidly suppress the body's metabolic demands, preserve the brain and other organs while surgeons stop the bleeding, and then allow circulation to be restored with useful neurologic recovery. The intended advance is a reliably reversible period of protected circulatory standstill that creates time for definitive repair.

Profound cooling is the experimental approach represented in the supplied evidence. Emergency preservation and resuscitation would connect rapid cooling, a protected interval for repair, and controlled restoration of circulation into one treatment sequence. A 2007 pig experiment supports parts of this technical premise, but its improved survival accompanied substantial neurologic impairment. It therefore does not demonstrate the complete proposed capability.

significance.text: Conditional impact judgment: reliable preservation could change the sequence of trauma care by creating a treatment window after circulatory arrest, during which repairable bleeding could be controlled before full resuscitation. Its direct benefit would be a chance of discharge with useful brain function for patients whose injuries could be repaired within that window. This would be a major surgical advance because preservation would make definitive repair possible under circumstances in which ongoing loss of organ viability otherwise constrains treatment.

Survival alone would not establish this benefit. In the inspected pig-study abstract, emergency preservation improved nine-day survival, but surviving treated animals had substantial neurologic deficits. The revolutionary claim therefore depends on achieving both successful repair and meaningful recovery, rather than merely restarting circulation or extending short-term survival. Effectiveness in human traumatic exsanguination remains unestablished by the supplied evidence.

Conditional downstream possibilities include a longer interval for complex emergency repair and, if separately justified, applications to planned bloodless surgery. Those extensions would require their own evidence about patient selection, acceptable risk and recovery. Emergency salvage after blood-loss arrest differs from planned circulatory arrest in a stable patient; evidence from either setting cannot automatically establish safety in the other. The supplied material does not substantiate the earlier background assertion about existing elective aortic-surgery practice or quantify mortality in the proposed trauma population.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is preservation that remains reversible across the entire emergency sequence: cooling must begin quickly enough to retain recoverable organ function, protection must last long enough for operative hemostasis, and reperfusion and rewarming must yield sustained circulation with useful neurologic recovery. These are engineering and clinical requirements inferred from the proposed treatment. The supplied evidence does not establish a human time limit for initiating preservation or a dependable duration for the protected repair window.

A major translational barrier is the difference between arrest with blood volume maintained and arrest after traumatic exsanguination. The inspected 2007 experiment used normovolemic ventricular fibrillation, so it does not establish whether the method can protect a patient who has also suffered hemorrhagic shock, tissue injury and ongoing bleeding. Cooling, surgical access, hemostasis, perfusion support and subsequent resuscitation would have to work together under those conditions. Neurologic impairment in the experiment shows that the demonstrated survival improvement falls short of the required organ protection.

Additional proposed barriers include controlling bleeding during profound cooling and preventing injury during restoration of blood flow and temperature. The earlier research identified hypothermia-associated coagulopathy as a potential conflict with hemostasis, but the retained evidence does not establish that assertion or its magnitude in this setting. It likewise does not establish that profound hypothermia is the most developed preservation approach. These remain questions to evaluate, rather than grounds for discarding the concept.

current_state.text: A 2007 laboratory study randomized 13 pigs after 15 minutes of normovolemic ventricular fibrillation. Six received emergency preservation using a cold saline aortic flush and hypothermic stasis, and seven received conventional resuscitation; the protocol subsequently used cardiopulmonary bypass. The inspected abstract reports brain temperature falling from 38.5 ± 0.2 °C to 16.7 ± 2.5 °C within 235 ± 27 seconds. Nine-day survival was five of six in the preservation group versus one of seven controls. This demonstrates rapid cooling and improved short-term survival in that specific laboratory model, not efficacy after traumatic blood loss or in humans.

The surviving preservation-group animals had a neurologic deficit score of 45%, with an interquartile range of 35–50%; the study defined 0–10% as normal. Thus, the survival result did not demonstrate normal neurologic recovery. The evidence available through the supplied review is the study abstract, which supports these reported outcomes but provides only partial access to the experiment and its methods.

The supplied 2002 citation concerns learning and memory after induced asanguineous hyperkalemic hypothermic arrest in a swine model of traumatic exsanguination, making it more directly relevant to blood-loss trauma. Earlier research reported preserved learning and memory and an indexed result of 80% survival after 60 minutes of shock. However, no source text was retained for the validated review to assess the protocol, denominators, neurologic measurements or those quantitative claims. These remain unverified reports in the supplied research; the missing text is not evidence that the results are false.

The supplied materials identify the EPR-CAT registry entry, NCT01042015, as the relevant human trauma study. Earlier research described University of Maryland sponsorship, a 2016 start, planned enrollment of about 20 patients, a discharge endpoint without major disability, and termination because enrollment was too slow, with primary completion dated November 21, 2025. The retained registry extraction contains only interface text and cannot verify those study-specific details. Earlier search indexes also disagreed about the last update date, listing December 17, 2025 and June 16, 2026. Consequently, the supplied evidence cannot establish the trial's current enrollment, disposition or human outcomes.

The earlier research reported finding no peer-reviewed human outcome paper, but the supplied search record is empty. It therefore cannot establish whether such a publication was available as of November 1, 2026, or support the broader assertion that no human study has ever demonstrated survival without major disability. The supported conclusion is narrower: the supplied, assessable evidence does not demonstrate successful human trauma preservation with meaningful neurologic recovery.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: prospectively study adults with penetrating trauma who lose vital signs within minutes of hospital arrival and do not regain a pulse with standard care. Emergency preservation, definitive repair and delayed resuscitation should produce survival to discharge with Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended greater than 5 at a prespecified rate exceeding a justified comparator for that population. This is a proposed outcome definition, not a verified attribution to EPR-CAT or an established completion standard. The comparator, clinically meaningful effect size and ethical justification should be specified before outcomes are assessed; the supplied evidence does not support using a historical survival rate of only a few percent without further substantiation.
completion_criteria.label: Discharge survival rate with GOSE >5 exceeds a justified comparator

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and reproducibility requirements: assess neurologic function at 6–12 months, alongside sustained survival and clinically important organ dysfunction. Report all eligible, attempted and treated cases so that inability to initiate preservation or complete repair remains visible in the results. Reproduction by independent teams and across centers would provide stronger evidence that success depends on a transferable procedure rather than a single team's circumstances.
completion_criteria.label: 6–12-month neurologic outcomes reported with complete case accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: record the preceding shock and no-flow intervals, time to cooling, temperature achieved, duration of standstill, injury pattern, time to hemostasis, and complications during reperfusion and rewarming. Convincing demonstrations should establish the range of injuries and treatment delays within which meaningful recovery is reproducible. Finite studies would demonstrate breadth within those tested conditions, not universal reversibility after arbitrary blood loss, arrest duration or tissue damage.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible recovery boundaries established across injuries and treatment delays

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: SUR-03, Life-sustaining cryobanking of human-scale organs, has the closest preservation overlap. Both require suppressing injury during interrupted circulation and recovering function afterward. SUR-08 concerns an acutely injured whole patient, a short emergency repair interval and neurologic recovery; SUR-03 concerns storing organs for later use. Success in organ storage would not by itself establish reversible whole-body preservation after trauma.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-04, Restoration of volitional function after complete spinal cord transection, and SUR-05, Adult surgical wounds that heal by regeneration rather than fibrosis, address recovery from established injury. SUR-08 primarily seeks to preserve recoverable tissue while the cause of arrest is repaired. Preservation cannot be assumed to reverse a severed spinal cord or produce regenerative wound healing.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-06, Autonomous completion of whole operations at expert level; SUR-07, Incisionless resection and reconstruction inside the closed body; SUR-10, Cell-identity-selective extirpation inside an organ that keeps working; and SUR-11, Real-time cellular and molecular vision of the intact operative field, concern how surgery is performed or guided. Such capabilities might eventually assist repair within a protected interval, but none inherently supplies metabolic preservation. Conversely, SUR-08 would not establish autonomy, incisionless access, selective cell removal or molecular visualization.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-01, Operational donor-specific tolerance for the transplants patients actually receive, and SUR-02, Destination-therapy solid-organ xenotransplantation, address transplantation and graft survival. SUR-09, Living, perfused autologous replacements for complex parts that grafts do not supply, and SUR-12, Life-sustaining autologous solid organs assembled for implantation, address replacement tissues and organs. These concepts could intersect with preservation and perfusion, but they solve replacement or compatibility problems. SUR-08 seeks to retain the injured patient's existing organs through emergency repair and resuscitation.

unresolved_issues: The 2002 study's full methods and results are unavailable in the retained material, leaving the reported 80% survival after 60 minutes of shock and preservation of learning and memory unverified.

EPR-CAT's sponsor, start date, planned and actual enrollment, exact endpoint, termination status, stopping reason and primary completion date require substantive registry evidence. The conflicting indexed update dates are unresolved.

The supplied search record cannot determine whether peer-reviewed human outcomes were available as of November 1, 2026, or whether meaningful human neurologic recovery has been demonstrated elsewhere.

Human organ-injury timing, the magnitude of cooling-associated coagulopathy in this setting, the comparative maturity of preservation approaches and background elective aortic practice are not established by the supplied evidence.
A justified clinical comparator, meaningful treatment effect, ethical study design and reproducible limits for delay, injury severity and preservation duration remain to be specified.

The review recommended removing unverifiable study and registry assertions. They are instead retained as explicitly unverified earlier reports to preserve the research's quantitative detail and uncertainty, without treating them as established findings.

brief.title: Buying time for surgery after fatal blood loss
possible: Someone whose heart stops after catastrophic bleeding could gain a protected window for emergency surgery. Doctors would rapidly cool the body to slow its demand for energy, repair the bleeding, then restore circulation and warmth.
The goal is to leave hospital with useful brain function after an otherwise unsurvivable interruption of blood flow.
why: For patients with repairable injuries, this would change the order of emergency care. Surgeons could stop the bleeding before fully restarting circulation, while the brain and other organs remain protected.

sources.who: Researchers studying traumatic blood loss in pigs
sources.showed: This animal study examined learning and memory after cooling and temporarily stopping circulation in pigs with traumatic blood loss.
sources.cited_for: It addresses preservation in a model involving traumatic blood loss.
sources.not_established: It does not establish reliable recovery in people after traumatic blood loss.

sources.showed: Rapid cooling improved short-term survival after cardiac arrest in pigs whose blood volume was maintained. Surviving treated animals had substantial brain impairment.
sources.quote: EPR is feasible in an experimental pig model and improves survival after prolonged cardiac arrest in pigs.
sources.cited_for: Cooling can improve survival after prolonged cardiac arrest in an animal experiment.
sources.not_established: The experiment did not demonstrate useful brain recovery after traumatic blood loss or effectiveness in humans.

sources.showed: EPR-CAT is a human study of emergency preservation and resuscitation after cardiac arrest caused by trauma.
sources.cited_for: It represents clinical investigation of preservation after traumatic cardiac arrest.
sources.not_established: Successful human treatment with meaningful brain recovery remains unestablished.

shown: Andreas Janata and collaborators tested rapid cooling in a small study involving 13 pigs. Cooling improved short-term survival, but surviving treated animals had substantial brain impairment. The animals had not lost blood, leaving a major gap between this experiment and emergency treatment for catastrophic bleeding.
missing: The full sequence needs to protect people through cooling, bleeding repair and restored circulation, with useful brain recovery.
A dependable repair window after traumatic blood loss needs to be established.
Safe restoration of blood flow and warmth needs to preserve sustained heart function and avoid major organ injury.

milestones.label: Hospital survival with useful brain recovery exceeds a justified comparison
milestones.explanation: A prospective trauma study would have to beat a justified comparison in discharge survival with a brain-recovery score above 5. This would test whether preservation and repair deliver meaningful clinical benefit.

milestones.label: Lasting recovery is reported with every case counted
milestones.explanation: Follow-up within the following year would have to report brain function, survival and organ problems, counting every eligible, attempted and treated case. Independent teams would strengthen confidence that others can repeat the success.

milestones.label: Recovery limits are reproducible across injuries and treatment delays
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to establish which injuries and delays allow repeatable recovery, including complications during restored blood flow and warming. This would define when the procedure can reliably help.

uncertain: How much delay and prior blood-loss shock can organs tolerate before preservation becomes ineffective?
How much does profound cooling interfere with stopping bleeding in this setting?
Which comparison group and size of benefit would make a clinical result convincing?

page.title: Emergency preservation and resuscitation for traumatic cardiac arrest
page.definition: Emergency preservation and resuscitation (EPR) aims to preserve the brain and other organs when traumatic blood loss has stopped the heart and standard resuscitation has failed. In the EPR-CAT protocol for penetrating injuries, ice-cold saline infused into the aorta rapidly cools the patient toward a brain temperature of about 10 °C. Once surgeons stop the bleeding, a heart-lung machine restores circulation and rewarms the patient. The aim is survival without major disability.

goal.need: Across 24 studies of emergency thoracotomy after blunt or penetrating trauma, only 7.4% of 4,620 patients survived. When blood loss stops the heart, even direct cardiac massage has little blood to circulate. Rapid cooling could lower the brain’s need for oxygen and give surgeons time to stop the bleeding before permanent injury occurs. For a patient with a repairable wound who can be cooled in time, that could mean surviving without major disability.

completion.title: An EPR-treated trauma patient leaves hospital with a Glasgow Outcome Scale–Extended score above 5.
completion.criterion: An EPR-CAT-eligible patient with penetrating-trauma cardiac arrest unresponsive to emergency thoracotomy undergoes preservation, bleeding repair and delayed resuscitation, then survives to hospital discharge with Glasgow Outcome Scale–Extended (GOSE) >5. GOSE measures functional recovery on eight levels; scores 6–8 qualify, including upper moderate disability.
completion.set_by: EPR-CAT investigators, Master Human Use Protocol, version 6, 26 April 2016, primary endpoint.
completion.threshold_quote: survival to hospital discharge without major disability (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended >5)
completion.basis: The FDA recommended this discharge endpoint for EPR-CAT. A qualifying discharge establishes success for that patient. The protocol called for comparison with concurrent or historical controls and specified no minimum survival rate establishing clinical effectiveness.

milestones.title: Pigs recover neurologic function and learning after 60 minutes of hypothermic preservation.
milestones.criterion: After uncontrolled bleeding from a thoracic aortic injury, pigs undergo vascular repair during 60 minutes at a core temperature of 10 °C on low-flow cardiopulmonary bypass. Over six weeks of follow-up, survivors must recover neurologic function on the study’s 75-point scale. Previously untrained animals must learn a color-coded food-retrieval task comparably to controls, and pretrained animals must retain the task.
milestones.set_by: Uniformed Services University investigators, published swine experimental protocol and cognitive endpoints, 2002; a model-specific test, not a regulatory preclinical standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: compared with control animals (n = 15), and 4 preoperatively trained animals were tested for memory retention postoperatively.

milestones.title: An eligible trauma patient receives the EPR-CAT intra-aortic cold saline flush.
milestones.criterion: In a patient who meets EPR-CAT eligibility criteria and remains pulseless after emergency thoracotomy for penetrating trauma, the trained team begins the protocol’s ice-cold saline infusion into the aorta.
milestones.set_by: EPR-CAT investigators, published clinical feasibility protocol and investigator’s description of EPR initiation.
milestones.threshold_quote: EPR is initiated via an intra-aortic flush of ice-cold saline solution.

milestones.title: An EPR patient reaches 10 °C at the eardrum or nasopharynx and below 30 °C rectally.
milestones.criterion: During EPR induction, temperature reaches 10 °C at either the tympanic membrane (eardrum) or the nasopharynx (behind the nose), and rectal temperature is below 30 °C. The first reading estimates brain temperature. The rectal reading assesses whole-body cooling.
milestones.set_by: EPR-CAT investigators, final clinical protocol published in 2017.
milestones.threshold_quote: Cooling will continue until Tty or Tnp is 10°C, and rectal temperature is less than 30°C.

milestones.title: An EPR-treated trauma patient returns to normal temperature without extracorporeal life support.
milestones.criterion: After bleeding control and delayed resuscitation, an EPR patient returns to normal body temperature without extracorporeal life support (ECLS), external support for circulation and oxygenation.
milestones.set_by: EPR-CAT investigators, Master Human Use Protocol, 26 April 2016, end of experimental treatment.
milestones.threshold_quote: rewarmed to normothermia and is not on ECLS.

milestones.title: Dogs recover normal neurologic function after 60 minutes of circulatory arrest at 15 °C.
milestones.criterion: After 30 minutes of hemorrhagic shock at a mean arterial pressure of 40 mm Hg, dogs are cooled to 15 °C on cardiopulmonary bypass. After 60 minutes of circulatory arrest, bypass restores blood flow and rewarms them. Recovery requires survival beyond 72 hours and a best neurologic deficit score of 0% during observation.
milestones.set_by: University of Pittsburgh investigators, 60-minute group and neurologic deficit scale in the 1990 canine protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: After circulatory arrest of 60 (Group 1), 90 (Group 2), or 120 (Group 3) minutes

milestones.title: Surgeons control an EPR patient’s bleeding and restore blood flow on cardiopulmonary bypass.
milestones.criterion: After cold preservation, the surgical team achieves hemostasis, meaning control of bleeding, and uses cardiopulmonary bypass to restore blood flow and begin rewarming.
milestones.set_by: EPR-CAT investigators, Master Human Use Protocol, version 6, transition from hemostasis to reperfusion.
milestones.threshold_quote: Once hemostasis has been achieved, CPB will be initiated

not_found: No published human cooling, recovery without extracorporeal support, discharge GOSE or long-term outcomes were located in PubMed-indexed papers and web searches.
The 2002 publisher full text could not be opened; its PubMed abstract leaves detailed cognitive and neurologic scoring methods unverified.
Searches of FDA material, guidelines and EPR-CAT documents found no minimum human success rate defining clinical effectiveness.
No public EPR-CAT report located gives actual enrollment or the total number of patients who received the cold flush.

results.finding: Among 6 EPR-treated pigs, the 5 day-9 survivors had a median neurologic deficit score of 45%.
results.detail: The reported neurologic scores show persistent impairment. The study reports no food-retrieval learning or retention results.
results.quote: Their neurologic deficit score was 45% (interquartile range 35, 50) and histologic damage score was 142 (interquartile range 109, 159).

results.finding: Of 26 pigs treated with hypothermic preservation, 22 survived to six weeks with intact neurologic function and normal learning capacity.
results.quote: All surviving animals were neurologically intact, displayed normal learning capacity, and had no longterm organ dysfunction.

results.finding: Of 40 swine enrolled, all 17 survivors were neurologically intact and showed normal learning after hypothermic arrest.
results.quote: All the surviving animals were neurologically intact, displayed normal learning capacity, and had no long-term organ dysfunction.

results.finding: Dogs in the 60-minute arrest group (15 dogs across all groups) had best neurologic deficit scores of 0 ± 0%.
results.quote: All dogs survived greater than 72 hours. Best neurologic deficit scores (ND) (0% = normal, 100% = brain death) were 0 +/- 0% (normal) in Group 1, 10 +/- 8% (mild disability) in Group 2, and 27 +/- 24% in Group 3.
